mechanism: An attacker runs a second MCP server advertising tools whose names, descriptions and schemas imitate a legitimate provider's. The client's LLM picks tools from metadata alone, which is not bound to a verified server identity, so the request resolves to the attacker's tool. The paper frames it as an optimisation over metadata and measures it across five LLM clients, finding exact-name collision plus matching description and schema is strongest.
claim: Tool-provider misbinding can route a request to an attacker-controlled MCP tool without compromising host, model, server or network.
why_not_testable: Needs LLM clients to select tools, and there is no local LLM or keyless model.
needs: An LLM client with MCP support
one_line: Two MCP servers advertising the same tool name can steal an agent's request, because tool metadata carries no verified provider identity.
idea_why: Selection by unauthenticated text metadata is a plain design gap and the collision case follows directly from it.
breakdown: To check it here, stand up two toy MCP servers with an identical tool name and different descriptions, connect both to a Claude Code session, and record which one gets called across repeated prompts. That tests Proteus's own exposure since its sessions load several MCP servers. Defence is namespacing by server and pinning allowed servers, which is configuration rather than a build.

mechanism: For a blocked agent tool call, the minimal sufficient reason is the smallest set of facts that forces the decision, computed exactly by a deletion algorithm: drop one fact at a time and keep it only if the decision flips. Models are scored against that ground truth, then a 4B model is fine-tuned on traces of the algorithm. The student learns a fixed probing schedule that stays sufficient but not minimal on unseen policies.
claim: A 4B model trained on 2000 algorithm traces hits 92% on its own policy, but only 48% minimality on three unseen policies.
why_not_testable: Needs model fine-tuning and LLM answers, neither available keyless tonight.
one_line: Training a small model on an exact deletion algorithm taught it a fixed schedule that did not carry over to unseen policies.
idea_why: Deletion-based minimal sufficient reasons are standard and the transfer failure is a plausible finding.
breakdown: The deletion algorithm itself is a few lines and could be run on a toy policy to produce audit explanations for the hook's deny reasons. The training half needs a GPU and a 4B model, which is not here. Proteus could borrow the algorithm for its own hook logs without any model.
